classification.difficultyReason: Proves a general relationship between a quadratic-divisor remainder and the line through two polynomial values.

content.prompt: Suppose we divide a polynomial $P(x)$ by $(x-a)(x-b)$ for $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $a\ne b$. Prove that the remainder determines the line joining the points $(a,P(a))$ and $(b,P(b))$.

answer.short:
$$y=R(x)=\frac{P(b)-P(a)}{b-a}x+\frac{bP(a)-aP(b)}{b-a}.$$

The remainder has degree less than 2 and satisfies $R(a)=P(a)$ and $R(b)=P(b)$, so its graph is the required line.
answer.worked:
Since the divisor has degree 2, write the remainder as $R(x)=Cx+D$. Then
$$P(x)=(x-a)(x-b)Q(x)+Cx+D.$$
Substituting $x=a$ and $x=b$ gives
$$\begin{align*}P(a)&=Ca+D,\\P(b)&=Cb+D,\\P(b)-P(a)&=C(b-a).
\end{align*}$$
Since $a\ne b$,
$$\begin{align*}C&=\frac{P(b)-P(a)}{b-a},\\D&=P(a)-\frac{a(P(b)-P(a))}{b-a},\\D&=\frac{bP(a)-aP(b)}{b-a}.
\end{align*}$$
Therefore,
$$R(x)=\frac{P(b)-P(a)}{b-a}x+\frac{bP(a)-aP(b)}{b-a}.$$
The graph $y=R(x)$ is a straight line passing through $(a,P(a))$ and $(b,P(b))$. These points have distinct horizontal coordinates, so this is their unique joining line.
